newsitem.title: USA: U.S. manufacturers challenge strong dollar policy.
newsitem.headline: U.S. manufacturers challenge strong dollar policy.

text.p: U.S. business leaders and trade experts Tuesday accused Japan of manipulating currencies for its own competitive advantage and called on the Clinton administration to do something to stop it.
"The Japanese, and to some extent the Europeans ... seem to be looking to export away their problems," National Association of Manufacturers President Jerry Jasinowski said.

He told a conference sponsored by the Economic Strategy Institute that his association has trimmed its forecast of U.S. export growth next year by about 30 percent because of the dollar's strength and the weak economic growth abroad.
The manufacturers' association now expects U.S. exports to grow by about seven percent next year, instead of the 10 percent it had previously been forecasting, Jasinowski said.

Michael Farren, a vice president at Xerox Corp and a former U.S. trade official, echoed Jasinowski's remarks about Japan's alleged currency manipulation. "This has been very much a yen problem, not a dollar problem," he said.

The dollar has risen some 40 percent against the yen since hitting a record low of 79.75 yen in April of last year. It briefly appreciated to close to 115 yen earlier this month, before falling back on suggestions by a senior Japanese official that its rise against the yen might be about to end.
But Lawrence Chimerine, chief economist at the Economic Strategy Institute, warned the United States against being fooled by that.

He suggested that Tokyo may have temporarily jawboned the dollar back down ahead of a meeting later this month between President Clinton and Japanese Prime Minister Ryutrao Hashimoto on the fringes of a gathering of leaders from the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation group.
